stories.summary: UH researchers studying 1,400 adults found high heavy metal and chemical exposure linked to abnormal lung function, though the share caused directly by the fires could not be determined.
stories.text: For some, recovery from the wildfires of 2023 may have serious health consequences. New research has found elevated levels of potentially harmful metals in Maui residents as far out as a year and a half after the fires. Researchers say burned buildings, vehicles, and electronics may have contributed to the exposure, although the study could not determine how much came directly from the fires because comparable pre-fire data does not exist.

stories.headline: Maui Huliau segment on managing tourism and its limits
stories.summary: Speakers discuss tourism growing without boundaries, carrying capacity, regenerative tourism and the industry's kuleana to Maui.
stories.text: Tourism was starting in the 60s. Airplanes came in, more tourism came, and then we didn't manage it properly. It got away, became the problem child that wasn't given boundaries. So now we are having to deal with this problem without any boundaries and trying to put boundaries into an industry that is used to just running free. You know, I know that there's visitors that come that have become family to us. But then there's always some of them that say, I'm entitled. I can go over here and I can go over there. I can cross the private property. You know, there's a book out there that tells them to do those things. And local people started realizing, wow, we've given up our spots to tourism. The spots we were enjoying as kids. But there is a way we can share the spaces. You talk story, you introduce your friend who's coming in with you, grandma bringing my friend. All of that is common decency and human manners. Do you know I'm paying your bill? Because I'm spending a thousand, you know, twenty thousand dollars on my vacation. I am entitled for you to serve me. But if we switch that and say, I'm here to help, I want to learn, I want to take those lessons home. I want to change my home for someplace better. Tourism is here to stay. We need it. It's part of our economy. It's not going away. So how can we work within it? When COVID happened, there was a lot of meetings on how we're going to change tourism. We're moving towards regenerative tourism. We have all these different types, ecotourism, agrotourism, we have all kinds of different tourism. We have a carrying capacity, which is like a cup full of water. The cup is already full, but we keep pouring water into it. And when you spill over, in fact, you have problems. Who's going to clean it up? There's got to be more education almost at every two steps to be able to teach from this perspective. If it wasn't for these native ecosystems and the Hawaiian culture, Maui would just be like anywhere else. Basically, the tourism industry has a kuleana to Maui and to make it so that Maui will remain a really amazing place for people to live, for people to want to come and visit.

stories.text: When the fire happened, there was a group of us that founded Roots Reborn that noted that from the previous natural disasters and sort of hostile political administrations, we learned that our immigrant community tends to be under-resourced and underrepresented at the decision-making tables. And when people are helping out with COVID relief or fire kūpuna You know, we're not going to make, we can't change on such a macro scale that everyone's going to feel safe, but what we're trying to do is make our community feel safer and be safer. Roots Reborn has developed a really cool network of volunteers who will respond to the first, we have a hotline number and they will respond to the first reports of ice activity and our volunteers will actually chase down the tip and make sure that it's real because what What we don't want is people on social media saying, oh, ISIS here at Walgreens or whatever, and it's not true. Because when they are here, people don't go to work, they don't go to school, they don't leave their houses. And so what we really want to do is help keep the community safe, but also keep them tranquilo because it's not helpful when everybody's freaking out.

stories.text: Lahaina Luna High School will host Paradise High School of California for a historic Unity Bowl this Saturday, September 5th, at 6 p.m. The game, themed Two Towns, One Spirit, brings together communities both devastated by deadly wildfires. Paradise was devastated by California's deadliest wildfire in 2018, while Lahaina suffered the deadliest U.S. wildfire in more than a century back in August of 2023.
